name: Arjun's body clock and water after a long flight

parameters.label: Time zones crossed
parameters.explain: The more time zones you cross, the more likely jet lag is — and the longer it lasts.

parameters.label: Nights since landing
parameters.explain: The body clock catches up a little each day — roughly a day for each time zone crossed.

parameters.label: Direction of the flight
parameters.explain: Flying east, when you 'lose' hours, is usually harder to adjust to than flying west.

parameters.label: Hours outdoors in morning daylight
parameters.explain: Sunlight is one of the strongest signals that sets the body clock, so the right light helps it shift faster.

parameters.label: Water drunk on the flight
parameters.explain: Cabin air is dry, so the body loses more water than usual just by breathing; not drinking enough leaves you slightly dehydrated.

parameters.label: Flight length
parameters.explain: Every hour in dry cabin air adds to the water lost.

parameters.label: Body weight
parameters.explain: The same water loss is a bigger share of a smaller body.

parameters.label: Cabin humidity
parameters.explain: Aircraft cabin air is usually only 10–20% humidity — very dry. Drier air takes more water from your lungs and skin.

explain.summary: Arjun has two separate problems. His body clock is still set to Los Angeles, so at 3 a.m. in London his body thinks it's early evening — and the clock only catches up about one time zone a day. Separately, eleven hours of very dry cabin air and only two cups of water left him low on water. Water fixes the headache in hours; only time and daylight fix the clock.
rules: The body clock starts out of step by one hour for each time zone crossed.
It catches up about one hour a day; flying west and getting morning daylight make it a bit faster.
Minutes awake at night grow with how far out of step the clock still is.
Water lost on the flight grows with flight length and dry air; water drunk makes up some of it.
Water missing above about 1.5% of body weight makes a headache likely.

source.fact: It usually takes about a day to recover for each time zone crossed; the more time zones you cross, the more likely jet lag is.
Jet lag is especially likely when flying east; eastward travel is usually harder to adjust to than westward.
Sunlight is a key influence on the body's circadian rhythms (its internal clock).
Humidity is low in planes, and not drinking enough water on a flight can leave you slightly dehydrated.
Aircraft cabin air is typically dry, usually 10–20% humidity, and pressurised to the equivalent of about 8,000 feet.
Signs of dehydration include extreme thirst, urinating less, dark-coloured urine and dizziness.

choice.what: The clock catches up 1 hour a day flying east and 1.5 hours a day flying west
choice.why: Matches 'about a day per time zone' and 'east is harder'; the westward speed is a teaching value.

choice.what: Each hour of morning daylight speeds adjustment by 15%
choice.why: Light is the strongest clock signal, but how much it helps depends on timing; the size here is illustrative.

choice.what: About 16 minutes awake at night for each hour the clock is still out of step
choice.why: Gives about two hours awake on the first night after eight time zones, as in the case. Real nights vary a lot.

choice.what: Water loss is a baseline plus extra for drier air
choice.why: Breathing and skin lose more water in very dry air; the numbers give a loss of about 1.3 litres on an 11-hour flight.

choice.what: Headache 'likely' above about 1.5% of body weight
choice.why: Mild dehydration often brings headaches; there is no single cut-off, so this is a teaching line.

illustrative: Arjun's weight (45 kg), his two cups of water and his half-hour of daylight are made up for a fictional story.
Minutes awake at night is a teaching scale; real sleep after a flight is much more uneven.
provenance.studying: Exactly how fast the body clock shifts — and the best timing of light to speed it up — is still being studied and differs between people.

does: Shows two separate problems from one trip, each with its own fix and its own speed
Shows the body clock catching up a little each day, faster flying west or with daylight
Shows dry cabin air and too little drinking adding up to water lost
doesnt: Measure any real person — Arjun is fictional and the numbers are estimates
Plan anyone's real trip or sleep schedule
Include naps, caffeine, food, or seat comfort
limits.text: This is a simplified learning model. Real people vary with age, fitness and health. The numbers are illustrative, not measurements of any real person.
limits.wellbeing: If a headache doesn't go away after drinking water and resting, or you feel unwell after a flight, tell an adult.
